title: Adaptive number of Mirror codebooks
hypothesis: A development-selected residual stopping rule can assign shorter Mirror code sequences to lower-complexity functions and preserve quality at lower aggregate serialized bytes than fixed-depth codes; a native RVQ stopping rule is the direct control.
physical_object: one shared 16D basis and 4-stage additive decoder
mirror_coordinate: per-function active residual stage count and one quantized phase index per active stage
controls: adaptive Mirror depth selected by a development-only residual threshold
native learned full-vector residual VQ with fixed and adaptive depth

task.type: synthetic 16D function vectors with heterogeneous residual complexity
task.teacher: targets have 1, 2, or 4 nonzero orthogonal 2D phase components in a balanced shuffled mixture; amplitudes [1,.5,.25,.125]

development.allowed: select one residual threshold per method from the registered sweep by minimum bytes subject to mean NRMSE <= 0.08; no fresh-dependent changes

paid_objects: all code indices and per-function active-depth metadata

success_gate: On every fresh world, adaptive Mirror mean NRMSE <=0.08 and <=80% of fixed-depth R4 Mirror bytes, with lower mean active stages than 4; compare against adaptive native RVQ at the same quality and generic coefficient control.
failure_gate: Adaptive code savings fail the byte/quality gate, threshold does not select heterogeneous depths, or native/generic adaptive control matches or beats Mirror on quality-byte-compute frontier.
boundaries: Synthetic known orthogonal basis with heterogeneous component count only.
This tests rate allocation, not independent capacity or natural audio codec performance.
Threshold selected only on development worlds before fresh access.
